entities.name: Hassan ibn Thabit
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Hassan ibn Thabit (died 674 CE), an esteemed Arabian poet, emerged as a pivotal figure in the nascent Islamic community, earning the title 'Poet of the Prophet' (Sha'ir al-Rasul). Born into the Banu Khazraj tribe in Yathrib (later Medina), he initially gained renown in pre-Islamic Arabia for his eloquent verses, but his significance was irrevocably shaped by his conversion to Islam. He became the primary poetic voice defending the Islamic prophet Muhammad and the fledgling Muslim community against their detractors, particularly the Quraysh polytheists, during the tumultuous period of the early 7th century CE.

His poetic contributions were not merely aesthetic; they served as a crucial form of ideological and psychological warfare. Hassan ibn Thabit composed numerous panegyrics (madīḥ) celebrating Muhammad's virtues and the triumphs of Islam, while simultaneously crafting scathing lampoons (hijāʾ) against the Prophet's enemies. His verses chronicled key events of the sīra (Prophet's biography), including the Hijra, the Battle of the Trench (627 CE), and the Conquest of Mecca (630 CE), offering vivid, contemporary accounts that resonated deeply with the early Muslim faithful and demoralized opponents. Muhammad himself endorsed Hassan's poetic efforts, reportedly saying, 'Recite, O Hassan, for the Holy Spirit is with you.'

Hassan ibn Thabit's extensive diwan (collected works) became an indispensable primary source for later historians and biographers of the Prophet, such as Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Sa'd, preserving details of early Islamic history and culture that might otherwise have been lost. His style and themes influenced generations of subsequent Arabic poets, establishing a precedent for devotional Islamic poetry and the use of verse as a tool for religious propagation and communal solidarity. His work remains a foundational text in Arabic literature and a testament to the power of rhetoric in shaping historical narratives.
